newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: PM SAYS BUDGET HORROR STORIES TO BE EXPECTED
The Prime Minister, John Howard, says the next federal Budget will be sensible and balanced despite the usual shock-horror stories.
He says the Government won't be breaking any election promises and won't treat any section of the community unfairly but he has refused to rule out cuts to health spending.
In Parliament yesterday, the Opposition produced a leaked departmental report showing plans to save more than 1.3 billion dollars in the health budget.
TELSTRA WELL PLACED FOR PRIVATISATION: ALSTON
Communications Minister, Richard Alston, says Telstra's half-yearly financial results make it very well placed for privatisation.
Senator Alston says it's encouraging Telstra's profits actually rose by 16 per cent before the redundancy fund was taken into account.
Telstra's 38 percent drop in profits was heavily influenced by the one-billion dollars the telecommunications giant has set aside to finance redundancy payments.
Telstra recorded a profit, after tax and abnormal items, of 742-million dollars for the six months to December.
Senator Alston says its the second successive half-year there has been alignment between revenue growth and operating expenses.
STATE, TERRITORY LEADERS CALL FOR TAX REFORM
State and Territory leaders are discussing tax changes at state level but say it is essential for the Federal Government to act on tax reform as well.
Victorian Premier, Jeff Kennett, says working on the reforms is difficult for the states but they are urgent.
All leaders except Queensland's Rob Borbidge, have agreed to a proposal to abolish state Financial Institutions Duty - FID - and replace it with a national bank debit tax.
They say the Premiers Conference due in a fortnight should be limited to financial matters, but they also want discussions on native title urgently.
DRUG TESTING FOR POLICE RECRUITS
Australian Federal Police recruits will be drug tested from today.
The tests will be conducted during the recruitment process, and are part of a new force policy banning members from using illicit drugs.
The Federal Government says drug tests are a good way to handle a problem highlighted by the New South Wales Police Royal Commission.
WIND WARNINGS ISSUES ALONG QLD COAST
In Queensland, a strong wind warning has been issued from Cardwell in the north to Coolangatta in the south as Cyclone Justin continues moving slowly towards the coast.
The Weather Bureau says Justin is continuing to intensify in the Coral Sea, but is expected to remain well offshore.
It's bringing gale force winds and showers to exposed coastal areas and islands from Gladstone to Bowen.
Beaches at Mackay have been closed because of rough seas.
The system is currently 800 kilometres east of Cairns and 650 kilometres northeast of Mackay.
The Bureau's Manfred Greitschus says it's main impact will be on islands off the Capricorn coast where big swells may cause problems on top of high tide.
QUINN FRAUD TRIAL CONTINUING
The Supreme Court has heard former Coles Myer Chief Brian Quinn told the former head of maintenance, Graham Lanyon, to bury the cost of his home renovations, in maintenance accounts.
Mr Quinn is charged with conspiring with Mr Lanyon to defraud Coles Myer of millions of dollars to pay for renovations to his Melbourne home.
Mr Lanyon said he didn't call for quotes because of the nature of the work and how it was to be invoiced.

He said when the question of invoicing first arose, Mr Quinn told him he had spoken with the then chairman, Bevan Bradbury, and that the costs of the renovations would be buried in maintenance accounts.
He said when it came for the jobs to be paid for, the builder would state the months costs and he would invent false works being carried out at the head office.
OUTRAGE OVER ARTIST'S FALSE IDENTITY
The curator of an indigenous art show says she's outrage at the relevation that acclaimed Aboriginal artist Eddie Burrup is really well known white painter Elizabeth Durack.
A number of Durack paintings under the name of Burrup were included in the art show Native Title Now and have been entered in this year's Sulman Prize.
Curator Doreen Miller has told ABC Radio the deception is tragic.
Eighty-two-year old Durack asked art historian Robert Smith to reveal the true identity of Burrup in this month's edition of the Art Monthly magazine.
